variants.reconstruction:
%n ša šadî | šemūšu | māš[u(m)-ma]
#note: See @bib{RN117@863}: “The spelling @i{še-mu} for @i{šumu} was understood by von Soden as standing for @i{šᵉmu} (@i{AHw}, pp. 1274–5). However, according to I.J. Gelb @i{šumu} derives from older *@i{šimum} (@i{BiOr} 12 (1955), p.105; cf. Hebrew @i{šēm}), so this orthography might instead derive from an archaic or dialectal variant of the word. (…) Perhaps, in the end, the text will turn out to be corrupt (read @akk{<<ŠE>> šum₃-su₂}). However that may be, the singular possessive suffix here and in l. 42 (@i{bābšu}, unless the referent there is the sun) is at first glance difficult to reconcile with the plural possessive suffixes in ll. 40-1 (@i{elūšunu}, @i{irassunu}). The solution proposed is that the Twin Mountains were indeed two mountains, one in the west and one in the east (such is the clear implication of l. 45). The singular pronouns refer to the mountain Gilgameš has reached, the plural to the mountains as a pair. (…)”

variants.reconstruction:
%n tišīt | bē[rī | ...] | iltānu
#note: See @bib{RN117@867}: “The north wind perhaps symbolizes the draught which heralds Gilgameš’s approach to the far end of the tunnel.” See also @bib{foster2006review@310}: “[when] Gilgamesh comes out in the East, he feels a north wind in his face as he gets near the end of his run (…); my own idea is that the poet was thinking of the Tigris tunnel in Armenia.” On this line, see also @bib{RN612@44–45}, referring to an interpretation by Heimpel, according to which the north wind is the “kindling agent” for the sun.
